Ideally, in the digital world the cost to move money shouldn't be dependent on how much you are moving.

For the most part, this is true, the amount of a bitcoin transaction doesn't affect the fees.

With other forms of trust-free wealth transfer the costs are typically much higher to transport and store large sums because it attracts attackers.

This is somewhat true of cryptocurrency as well, but not to the same degree as something like gold.

For this reason, if bitcoin is seen as valuable enough, it could still be an effective store of value like gold for large amounts even if the fees are quite high.

I'd like to see more BTC scaling, but I think BTC may well end up more like digital gold than originally thought.

With sidechains and alt-coins being the equivalent of national currencies on top of gold in the crypto space. Gold is too costly to transact, so we use(d) representations of it instead.

This arrangement typically leads to counter-party risk, but crypto is quite magical.

It's very ironic. People used to say bitcoin is not a value store, it is a means of transaction. Between high fees and it's relative price stability (I guess not now) it's actually proved to be the opposite. It's a good value store and not a good transaction medium.

Etherium looks to be the best currency for transaction medium at the moment but people haven't diversified their coins. There is another reason to diversify your coins. Network congestion. If you want to make a purchase but bitcoin is going to charge you an arm just to move some money you should have another medium. You just want to protect your purchasing power at any moment.

That diversity also should apply to merchants. They especially have a high risk from network congestion if all of a sudden your customers aren't interested in doing business. If you currently accept bitcoin anywhere you should also accept ether. Ether currently has about half the total purchasing power of bitcoin so it's not like it's not like it is obscure.

It's one of those things where you need one to have the other.

A value store is no good if it is non transferrable.

I do think ether is one of the more interesting up and comers. It has a solid use case and seems like the devs know what they are doing.

The problem is it's value is entirely arbitrary. Things can have value even when they are very poor at transfer. Gold is an example. It's really not that liquid and you can pay a fair bit to sell it and it's not very trustworthy between individuals, but is still valued even though even bitcoin is more transferable. Antiques are another one. The trouble of two people being able to easily acknowleged what something is worth with little risk is considered an important aspect for a currency but no one would say antiques don't have a value.

So bitcoin can become an absolutely horrible currency and still have value.
